newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Olympics site at risk from toxic waste - Greenpeace.
newsitem.headline: Olympics site at risk from toxic waste - Greenpeace.

text.p: An area near the site of the 2000 Sydney Olympics has become "the new dioxin capital of the world", environmental organisation Greenpeace said on Tuesday.

Greenpeace said tests carried out on chemical storage drums discovered on the shores of Homebush Bay in western Sydney showed the same amount of dioxin contamination as Seveso, Italy, the site of a the world's first major dioxin accident in 1976.
"The drums are on the shores of Homebush Bay, within meters of the shoreline itself and just a kilometre away from the Olympic ferry terminal," a Greenpeace spokeswoman said.
However, a spokesman for the New South Wales state government said the issue was already being dealt with and he dismissed claims that Olympic facilities were under threat.

Greenpeace said the toxic waste in the 70 or so 200-litre drums at the site was believed to be waste material from a previous attempt to clean up a site formerly used by chemical giant Union Carbide, which operated a plant producing the herbicide 2,4,5-T at Homebush Bay until 1976.
The spokesman for state enviroment minister Pam Allan said the New South Wales Environment Protection Authority (EPA) had investigated the drums last week following a tip-off.
"They investigated the drums and found that they weren't stored in accordance with practices in the management of hazardous materials," the spokesman said.
He said the property owners, Bankers Trust, had been issued with a legally binding notice requiring the company to properly store the material on the site.
Water in Homebush Bay is well known for being contaminated and fishing in the bay has been banned for a number of years.

However, Greenpeace said a comprehensive cleanup and rehabilitation programme for Homebush Bay had not yet got under way and it warned that the commitment by Olympic organisers to a "green games" appeared to be waning.
"The 'Green Olympics' is beginning to look a distinctly muddy shade of brown," Greenpeace Olympics campaigner Michael Bland said in a statement.

"Unless the New South Wales government cleans up this area properly, athletes and visitors from all over the world will come metres of a site which has unacceptable levels of toxic waste," Bland said.
Greenpeace said dioxin levels in fish found in the bay among the highest it had ever encountered.
However, a spokesman for Minister for Ports Carl Scully said said rehabilitation options were being considered for the bay and there was plenty of time for the cleanup to be completed.
"We have had a large amount of testing and other work conducted there and the minister is in the final stages of developing options for remediation of the bay," he said.
"A decision will made on that shortly and ample time exists to address the situation with that time frame."
